content.text: If you place a metal spoon in a cup of hot tea, the handle soon becomes warm, even though it is not in direct contact with the hot liquid. If you touch a metal railing on a cold morning, it feels much colder than a wooden fence post, even though both are at the same temperature. These everyday observations are explained by thermal conduction, the transfer of thermal energy through a material without the material itself moving.

Conduction is one of the three main methods of thermal energy transfer (along with convection and radiation). In this lesson, we will explore the mechanism of conduction at the particle level, learn what makes some materials good conductors and others good insulators, and understand the practical applications of conduction.

Thermal conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a substance from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature, without the substance itself moving. The energy is transferred from particle to particle through vibrations and (in metals) through the movement of free electrons.

Conduction occurs in solids, liquids, and gases, but it is most effective in solids because the particles are closest together. It is least effective in gases because the particles are far apart and collide infrequently.

The Mechanism of Conduction in Non-Metals
In non-metallic solids (such as glass, wood, and plastic), conduction occurs through
When one end of a solid is heated, the particles at that end gain kinetic energy and vibrate more vigorously.
These vibrating particles collide with their neighbouring particles, transferring some of their kinetic energy to them.
These neighbours, now vibrating more vigorously, pass the energy on to their neighbours, and so on.
Energy is transferred along the solid from the hot end to the cold end, particle by particle.
This process is relatively slow because each particle can only pass energy to its immediate neighbours. The particles do not move from their positions; they simply vibrate and pass energy along.
The Mechanism of Conduction in Metals
Metals are much better conductors than non-metals because they have an additional mechanism of energy transfer:

In a metal, the outer electrons of the atoms are not bound to individual atoms. Instead, they form a "sea" of free electrons that can move throughout the metal structure. These free electrons play a crucial role in conduction:
At the hot end of a metal, the free electrons gain kinetic energy and move faster.
These fast-moving electrons travel rapidly through the metal (much faster than vibrations can transfer energy through the lattice).
As the electrons move toward the cooler end, they collide with metal ions in the lattice, transferring their kinetic energy.
This causes the ions at the cooler end to vibrate more, increasing the temperature.

Because free electrons can move quickly through the entire metal, energy is transferred much faster than it could be by particle vibrations alone. This is why metals feel cold to the touch on a cold day: they conduct heat away from your warm skin very efficiently.

In metals, both free electrons and lattice vibrations contribute to conduction, but the free electron mechanism is much more significant. This is also why good electrical conductors (like copper and silver) tend to be good thermal conductors: both properties depend on having many free electrons.

Insulators work because their particles are either far apart (gases), irregularly arranged (amorphous solids), or connected by weak bonds that do not transfer vibrations efficiently. Most importantly, non-metals do not have free electrons, which removes the most effective mechanism of conduction.
is one of the best insulators available. Many practical insulating materials work by trapping small pockets of air:
Wool and fur contain air pockets between fibres
Expanded polystyrene contains tiny air bubbles
Fibreglass insulation contains air between glass fibres
Double glazing traps a layer of air or gas between two panes of glass
Cavity wall insulation fills the gap in a cavity wall with foam or mineral wool
Trapped air is a better insulator than free air because it cannot move and form convection currents (which would transfer heat more quickly).
Factors Affecting the Rate of Conduction
The rate at which thermal energy is conducted through a material depends on several factors:
Materials with higher thermal conductivity conduct heat faster. Metals conduct heat much faster than non-metals.
A larger cross-sectional area allows more energy to pass through per second. Think of it as having a wider path for the energy to travel along.
A shorter or thinner piece of material conducts heat faster because the energy has less distance to travel. This is why thin walls lose heat faster than thick walls.
A larger temperature difference between the hot and cold ends drives energy transfer faster. The rate of conduction is proportional to the temperature difference.

Rods of different materials (copper, iron, glass, wood) of the same length and diameter are coated with wax at one end. The other ends are placed in a flame or hot water bath. The wax melts fastest on the best conductor (copper) and slowest (or not at all) on the best insulator (wood). This demonstrates that different materials conduct heat at different rates.
Experiment 2: Water as a poor conductor

A test tube of water with an ice cube held at the bottom (weighted down with wire gauze) can be heated at the top until the water boils. The ice at the bottom barely melts, showing that water is a very poor conductor. The hot water at the top does not transfer its energy efficiently downward through conduction.

If a fine metal gauze is held over a Bunsen burner flame, the flame does not pass through the gauze. The gauze conducts heat away from the flame so efficiently that the gas on the other side of the gauze does not reach its ignition temperature. This principle is used in the Davy safety lamp for mines.

The base and sides of saucepans are typically made of metals like aluminium, copper, or stainless steel, which are good conductors. This allows heat from the stove to pass quickly and evenly into the food. Copper-bottomed pans are particularly prized because copper has very high thermal conductivity, giving very even heat distribution.

Electronic components like computer processors generate heat that must be removed. Metal heat sinks (usually aluminium) with fins are attached to the component. The metal conducts heat away from the component quickly, and the fins increase the surface area for the heat to be transferred to the air.
The engine's coolant passes through a metal radiator with many thin fins. The metal conducts heat from the coolant to the fins, where it is transferred to the air.
While the pan body is metal (a conductor), the handle is made of wood, plastic, or Bakelite (an insulator). This prevents heat from conducting to the handle, so it stays cool enough to hold.
Houses lose heat through walls, roofs, floors, and windows. Insulation reduces this heat loss:
Loft insulation (fibreglass or mineral wool) reduces heat loss through the roof
Cavity wall insulation (foam or mineral wool between inner and outer walls) reduces heat loss through walls
Double glazing (two panes with trapped air or argon between them) reduces heat loss through windows
Underfloor insulation reduces heat loss through the floor

Winter clothing works by trapping air between fibres. The trapped air acts as an insulator, reducing heat loss from the body. Multiple thin layers are more effective than a single thick layer because each layer traps a separate layer of air.
Made from insulating materials to prevent conduction of heat from hot dishes to your hands.
Used for hot drinks because polystyrene is an excellent insulator (it contains many trapped air pockets), keeping the drink hot and the outside of the cup cool.
A common question is why a metal bench feels colder than a wooden bench on a cold day, even though both are at the same temperature. The answer involves conduction:
. Both the metal and wood are at the ambient temperature (say,
When you sit on the metal bench, the metal rapidly conducts heat away from your body because it is a good thermal conductor. Your skin temperature drops quickly, and you feel cold.
When you sit on the wooden bench, the wood conducts heat away from your body very slowly because it is a good insulator. Your skin stays warmer for longer, and you feel less cold.
The sensation of "coldness" is actually a sensation of heat leaving your body, not a measurement of temperature.

Explain why copper is a better thermal conductor than wood, using the particle model.

Copper is a metal and has a large number of free electrons that are not bound to individual atoms. When one end of a copper rod is heated, these free electrons gain kinetic energy and move rapidly through the metal. As they collide with the metal ions in the lattice, they transfer energy to them, causing them to vibrate more. Because free electrons move very quickly, energy is transferred rapidly along the rod.

Wood is a non-metal and has no free electrons. Energy can only be transferred through vibrations of particles, where each particle passes energy to its neighbour through direct contact. This is a much slower process because each particle can only interact with its immediate neighbours, and the bonds between particles in wood are not very efficient at transmitting vibrations.
The combination of free electron conduction and lattice vibration in copper makes it a much better conductor than wood, which relies on lattice vibration alone.
Misconception 1: "Cold travels from cold objects to warm objects"
Cold is not a substance that travels. Thermal energy always flows from hot to cold. When you touch a cold metal railing, heat flows from your warm hand to the cold metal, not the other way around.
Misconception 2: "Metal objects are colder than their surroundings"

A metal chair in a room is at exactly the same temperature as the air, the carpet, and the wooden table in the same room (assuming thermal equilibrium has been reached). The metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your skin faster.

Insulators do not keep cold out. They slow down the transfer of thermal energy. A well-insulated house loses heat more slowly, so it stays warmer. But the insulation does not generate heat or actively block cold.
Misconception 4: "Conduction requires the material to move"

In conduction, the material does not move. Energy is passed from particle to particle through vibrations (and free electrons in metals). This distinguishes conduction from convection, where the material itself moves.
Misconception 5: "Thicker conductors conduct heat faster because they have more material"
This depends on the context. A thicker slab of material (greater
) actually conducts heat more slowly, because the energy has further to travel. However, a conductor with a larger cross-sectional area (
) conducts heat faster because there are more particles available to transfer energy in parallel.

While air has very low thermal conductivity, it is only a good insulator when it is trapped in small pockets. If air is free to move, it transfers heat by convection, which can be quite efficient. The best insulation materials trap air in tiny spaces, preventing convection.

Metals have a large number of free (delocalised) electrons

that are not bound to individual atoms. These free electrons can move rapidly through the metal lattice, carrying both thermal energy and electrical charge. In thermal conduction, fast-moving electrons at the hot end transfer kinetic energy to metal ions at the cooler end through collisions. In electrical conduction, the same free electrons carry charge when a potential difference is applied. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Multiple thin layers trap separate pockets of air between them.

Trapped air is an excellent insulator because it has very low thermal conductivity and cannot form convection currents. A single thick garment has fewer trapped air layers and may allow more air circulation within the fabric, reducing its insulating effectiveness. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Both the stone and carpet are at the same temperature, but stone is a much better thermal conductor than carpet.

When your bare foot touches stone, heat is conducted away from your skin rapidly, so your skin temperature drops quickly and you feel cold. Carpet is a poor conductor (it also traps air), so heat leaves your foot much more slowly and your skin stays warmer. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Copper first (highest thermal conductivity), then aluminium, then iron, then glass (lowest).

The drawing pins on the copper rod fall off first because copper conducts heat the fastest. Glass is such a poor conductor that the pins may not fall off at all within a reasonable time. — (comparison)
Trapped air cannot circulate and form convection currents
, so the only mechanism of heat transfer through it is conduction. Air has a very low thermal conductivity (

), making still, trapped air an excellent insulator. Free-moving air can form convection currents that transfer heat much more efficiently than conduction alone. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Snow and ice contain trapped air pockets, making them good thermal insulators.

The igloo blocks the wind (preventing convective heat loss) and the snow walls slow down conduction of heat from inside to outside. Body heat from the occupants warms the interior air, which is retained by the insulating snow walls. The temperature inside can be significantly warmer than outside, even though the walls are made of ice. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
